desc:
A single CPU uses preemptive shortest-remaining-time-first scheduling. Job i is given as jobs[i] = [arrival, burst]: it becomes available at time arrival and needs burst units of CPU time in total.

At every moment the CPU runs the available unfinished job with the smallest remaining time (ties: smaller index). When a job arrives whose remaining time is smaller than that of the running job, or equal with a smaller index, it takes over immediately, and the interrupted job keeps its remaining time. If no job is available the CPU idles until the next arrival. Return the time at which each job finishes, indexed like jobs.

jobs = [[0, 7], [2, 4], [4, 1], [5, 4]]
0..2 job 0 runs (5 left); at 2 job 1 (4) is shorter -> runs 2..4 (2 left)
at 4 job 2 (1) is shorter -> runs 4..5, done at 5
at 5: job 1 (2 left), job 3 (4), job 0 (5) -> job 1 runs 5..7, done at 7
job 3 runs 7..11, job 0 runs 11..16
answer = [16, 7, 5, 11]
hints: Simulating every time unit is far too slow for large arrival times, and the CPU may even idle for a long time. Only a few instants matter: arrivals and completions.
Between two consecutive arrival times the set of available jobs is fixed, so the CPU simply keeps working on the best job until it finishes or the next arrival occurs, whichever is first.

Sort the jobs by arrival. Keep a clock and a min-heap of (remaining, index). Push all arrived jobs, pop the best, and run it for min(remaining, next_arrival - clock). If it is not finished push it back with the reduced remaining time; otherwise record the finish time. If the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next arrival.
editorial: The schedule can only change at an arrival (a newcomer may preempt) or at a completion. Between those events the CPU works on the job with the smallest remaining time, so we can jump from event to event instead of stepping through unit times.

Maintain a clock t, the next unseen arrival, and a min-heap keyed by (remaining, index). After inserting every job with arrival ≤ t, pop the best job. If it can finish before the next arrival (t + remaining ≤ next_arrival) record t + remaining as its completion time. Otherwise run it until the next arrival and push the leftover back; the loop then inserts the new arrival and the heap decides whether it preempts.

Each arrival causes at most one preemption, so the number of loop iterations is at most 2n and the cost is O(n log n). The tie-break by index is encoded by the second tuple component. If no job is available, jump forward to the next arrival rather than stepping the clock.
solution:
import heapq


def completionTimes(jobs):
    n = len(jobs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (jobs[i][0], i))
    h = []
    done = [0] * n
    t = 0
    p = 0
    finished = 0
    while finished < n:
        if not h and t < jobs[order[p]][0]:
            t = jobs[order[p]][0]
        while p < n and jobs[order[p]][0] <= t:
            i = order[p]
            heapq.heappush(h, (jobs[i][1], i))
            p += 1
        rem, i = heapq.heappop(h)
        nxt = jobs[order[p]][0] if p < n else None
        if nxt is None or t + rem <= nxt:
            t += rem
            done[i] = t
            finished += 1
        else:
            heapq.heappush(h, (rem - (nxt - t), i))
            t = nxt
    return done
